full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an application filed under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 30-8-1999, passed by the learned Metropolitan Additional Sessions Judge, Dhaka, in Criminal Appeal No.1408 of 1999 dismissing the appeal and upholding the order of conviction and sentence dated 30-9-1995 passed by the Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka in CR Case No.2473 of 1994, should not be set aside. 

 2. The informant, Hazera Begum and the petitioner, Abdul Khaleque are workers under the Dhaka Municipal Corporation and live in neighbouring residential quarters. On 21-8-94 the petitioner had left an iron bed in front of the informant's door where her son-in-law brushed against it and got injured. The informant asked the petitioner to remove the bed, but he abused her instead. She also asked the petitioner wife to remove the bed, but she also failed to do so and at one point there was an altercation between the petitioner and the complainant, in the course of which the accused-petitioner kicked the complainant's abdomen. She fell to the ground and as she was getting up, he struck her on the head with a piece of wood (লোহা কাঠের টুকরা) causing bleeding injury. She became unconscious and was taken to Mitford Hospital where 19 stitches were required on her head. Initially an attempt was made to settle the matter, but since no compromise was reached, the informant lodged the case. 

 5. Mr Md Taherul Islam, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No.1, submitted that the prosecution was able to prove to the entire satisfaction of the Courts below that the petitioner inflicted the injury upon the informant and rightly convicted and sentenced the petitioner. He submitted that the evidence of the defence witness has corroborated the prosecution case that the petitioner inflicted injury upon the complainant and an attempt was made to compromise the matter. However, the complainant strongly refuted the claim that any compromise was ever reached and denied that she received any money. He pointed out that the Courts below have not believed the fact of compromise and that, being a concurrent finding of fact, should not be interfered with by this Court. He prays that the Rule may be discharged. 

 7. Having scrutinised the evidence on record, it thus appears to me that quite clearly an occurrence took place over such a mundane matter as the placing of an iron bed in the passage in front of the informant's door. It is also in evidence that an injury was caused to the complainant which required several stitches. The learned trial Judge saw and commented upon the injury, which he noticed on the head of the victim. However, no doctor was called to substantiate the extent of the injury nor the piece of wood, which was used to strike the victim, was produced before the Court. An injury certificate was produced and exhibited by the victim herself, but for it to have any evidentiary value the same must be proved in accordance with law and its veracity tested by examining the person who issued the certificate or at least some person in authority from the Emergency Department of Sir Salimullah Medical College Hospital. The other pieces of paper tending to show that treatment was received by the victim have not been exhibited at all in this case and cannot be considered as evidence. Thus, although I am inclined to accept that an occurrence took place and that the informant, who was the victim of the occurrence, received an injury on her head having been struck by the accused petitioner, I am not satisfied on the evidence on record about the extent of the injury. For the offence under section 324 to be proved it would have to be shown that the piece of wood was of such a size and weight that it could cause death of the victim. In the absence of such evidence, the offence under section 324 of the Penal Code is not proved. However, considering the evidence on record, there is no doubt that an offence under section 323 has been committed by the accused petitioner. 

 8. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the parties being inhabitants of the same Municipal residential quarters and the occurrence having arisen out of a trifling issue, I feel that a sentence of imprisonment is, at this stage, inappropriate and would not be of any benefit to any one, in particular bearing in mind that the accused is a first time offender and the injury was caused in the course of an altercation. It is unlikely that the petitioner would commit such an offence again. However, that is not to say that he should not be punished at all. In my view, the penal system of Bangladesh is essentially reformative in character as opposed to retributive. The provision afforded by the Probation of Offenders Ordinance, 1960 ("the Ordinance") is a prime example of such a penal policy. If a sentence of probation is imposed for a period of time, then it is likely to be more of a deterrent and will have a rehabilitating effect which will fulfil the intention of the legislature in promulgating section 5 of the said Ordinance. In such circumstances, I am inclined to pass an order under the provision of section 5 of the Ordinance. 

 9. It should be mentioned here that there is some confusion about the Ordinance. Some doubt that it still remains a valid law in Bangladesh; and others, that it applies only to cases involving first- time offenders who are sentenced to imprisonment for offences where the maximum sentence is of 2 years imprisonment. In this regard, I am grateful for the assistance rendered by Mrs Fahima Nasrin, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, learned Advocates Mr Anisul Hoque and Dr Shahdeen Malik and Mrs Jhama Jahin, Day Care Officer (Prison) of the Dhaka Central Jail. 

 11. Another apparent misconception is that the 1960 Ordinance only applies to cases of first-time offenders and where the offence is punishable with imprisonment for not more than two years. In fact, that restriction is applicable only to the provision in section 4 relating to conditional discharge, etc. On the other hand, section 5 provides for power of Court to make a probation order in certain cases. This provision is separate and distinct from section 4 and is not subject to those qualifications of that section. However, the applicability of the provision in section 5 is delimited by the exclusions mentioned therein. Section 5 of the Ordinance provides as follows: 

 "5. Power of Court to make a probation order in certain cases-(1) Where a Court by which- 

 (2) While making a probation order, the Court may also direct that the bond shall contain such conditions as in the opinion of the Court may be necessary for securing super- vision of the offender by the probation officer and also such additional conditions with respect to residence, environment, abstention from intoxicants and any other matter which the Court may, having regard to the particular circumstances of the case, consider necessary for preventing a repetition of the same offence or a commission of other offences by the offender and for rehabilitating him as an honest, industrious and law abiding citizen. 

 12. The facts of the instant case are such that a probation order would be most apt and suitable since it will have the likely effect of deterring the accused-petitioner from committing any further offence within the period of probation, which will allow also for his rehabilitation as an honest, industrious and law-abiding citizen, as is the intent and purport of the Ordinance. 

 15. Abdul Khaleque, accused in CR Case No. 2473 of 1994, is hereby directed to surrender before the trial Court within 1(one) month from communication of this order. The learned Magistrate is directed to implement this order, keeping in view the requirements of the Ordinance to ensure that the offender enters into a bond with sureties, and that the other requirements as mentioned in section 5 are fulfilled and complied. The Magistrate is further directed to explain to the petitioner that he will be bound to report to the Probation Officer as stipulated and if he fails to fulfil the conditions mentioned in this order, including the payment of compensation, then he will have to return to this Court and a sentence shall be passed in respect of the offence for which the probation order is made. It is further ordered that the compensation of Taka 1,000, if realised, be paid to the victim, Hazera Begum forthwith in accordance with section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Ordinance, 1960.
